notes: Bayes Rules! Bayes Rules! Exercises 18.5-18.8 (chapter-18): 18.6 asks for a 'hierarchical Poisson regression model of total_minutes by avg_points, starter, and games_played' with team the grouping variable; 18.7 redoes it with Normal and Negative Binomial likelihoods and 18.8 leaves the choice to the reader; priors in words only. An exercise, no worked fit. total_minutes is games_played times avg_minutes_played, so avg_minutes_played is ignored; starter codes games_started over half of games_played, and games_started is the open response of Exercise 18.9. A player traded during the season has a row per team and a TOT row that totals them (Kristine Anigwe), so team TOT holds totals of other rows; player_name is ignored as an id.

notes: Bayes Rules! Exercise 19.9 (chapter-19): bwc <- big_word_club %>% mutate(treat = as.factor(treat)); model score_pct_change by treat, age_months, private_school, esl_observed and free_reduced_lunch, 'accounting for there being multiple student participants per school_id'; priors in words only. An exercise, no worked fit. Kalil, Mayer and Oreopoulos (2020), ICPSR 117330.

formula: rides ~ user + temp_actual + weekend + humidity + weather_cat + (1 | date)
notes: Help page: daily observations, 267 each for registered and casual riders, so each date holds two rows. Bayes Rules! Chapter 11 (chapter-11) plots rides against temp_actual, weekend, humidity and weather_cat by user and splits the table by user (filter(user == 'casual')), fitting no model on it. Proposed: a Poisson model of rides by user type and the day's weather, date the grouping factor of the paired rows (a column that indexes a unit the rows repeat within, #133). Days from the UCI Bike Sharing data (Fanaee-T and Gama 2013).

RESPONSE INFERRED: the help page documents late-December Ontario counts of each species per year (1921-2017), one row per species and year, with no model. Bayes Rules! fits Normal, Poisson and Negative Binomial regressions only on its one-species subsets (bald_eagles in Exercises 12.5-12.9, loons). Proposed: the count with the person-hours as exposure and a species intercept. species_latin aliases species; count_per_hour and count_per_week are the count over hours.

notes: Bayes Rules! Chapter 17 (chapter-17): running <- cherry_blossom_sample %>% select(runner, age, net) %>% na.omit(); running_model_1 <- update(running_model_1_prior, prior_PD = FALSE), the prior model being stan_glmer(net ~ age + (1 | runner), family = gaussian) with these priors; Section 17.4 says 'we choose running_model_1' over running_model_2 with (age | runner), which adds 'little apparent change or benefit'. Chapter 15 introduces the table with a complete pooled stan_glm. gun is the alternate race time; the book drops rows without net.

Bayes Rules! Section 19.2 (chapter-19): climbers <- climbers_sub %>% select(peak_name, expedition_id, member_id, success, year, season, age, expedition_role, oxygen_used); climb_model_2 <- stan_glmer(success ~ age + oxygen_used + (1 | expedition_id) + (1 | peak_name), family = binomial), settled over climb_model_1 with the expedition intercept alone (the model of Section 18.1). The passed priors, normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = TRUE) for intercept and slopes and decov(reg = 1, conc = 1, shape = 1, scale = 1), are rstanarm's defaults. Expeditions nest in peaks; peak_id aliases peak_name and member_id is the row id. died and the death and injury details are other outcomes; injured stays, since Exercise 18.10 offers it as a predictor.

Bayes Rules! Exercise 16.2 (chapter-16, hierarchical models without predictors) asks whether farm_name and processing_method are grouping variables or predictors in a model of total_cup_points; batches repeat within farms, so farm_name groups. Exercise 17.14 (chapter-17) asks for a hierarchical model of total cup points over 'multiple batches from each of 27 farms' on coffee_ratings_small, a simplified version of this table excluded as derived, and leaves the predictors to the reader. Proposed: the one-way model of Chapter 16. total_cup_points sums the grades aroma to sweetness with clean_cup and a cupper score not in the table (CQI scoring), so the grades nearly determine it. species is row 2's response.

Bayes Rules! Exercise 18.1 (chapter-18) poses a hierarchical model of whether a batch is of the Robusta species by its flavor on coffee_ratings and leaves the grouping variable to the reader; farm_name is the grouping of row 1 (Exercises 16.2 and 17.14). total_cup_points is row 1's response.

Help page: one row per respondent of the popvssoda.com volunteer survey with the respondent's state and census region; pop marks the respondents whose word_for_cola is pop, so word_for_cola is ignored as the response's source. Bayes Rules! uses the table to illustrate Bayes' rule over regions and fits no model on it. Proposed: a logistic model with region and a state intercept; states nest in regions (an area factor with many levels groups, LGAclaims).

Cole', 'Kendrick Lamar')) %>% select(artist, album_id, popularity, valence), 'for illustrative purposes only'; Exercise 19.6 fits popularity by valence with 'random intercepts but not random slopes throughout', first by artist alone, then by artist and album; priors in words only. The help page cites Winter's tutorial (bodo-winter.net/tutorial/bw_LME_tutorial2.pdf) for the Winter and Grawunder (2012) data; its p. 8 fits politeness.model = lmer(frequency ~ attitude + (1|subject) + (1|scenario), data = politeness), subjects crossed with seven scenarios (the items), each in a polite and an informal attitude, frequency the pitch in Hz. The tutorial's next model adds gender, which voices lacks; subjects are coded A to F here.

Bayes Rules! Exercises 17.10-17.13 (chapter-17): a model in which 'baseline voice pitch differs from subject to subject' while the impact of attitude is similar among all subjects, a random intercept by subject; Exercise 16.13 analyses pitch without predictors. Priors in words only (a typical pitch around 200 Hz). An exercise, no worked fit.

StroupGLMM Exam3.9 (Stroup 2012, Example 3.9, p. 118): trt and loc as factors; glmmPQL(fixed = S2/Nbin ~ trt, random = ~1|loc, family = quasibinomial(link = 'logit')), the conditional binomial GLMM. The same page fits a Normal approximation lme(S2/Nbin ~ trt, random = ~1|loc), a fit with random = ~1|trt/loc whose trt:loc cells hold one row each (an observation-level term), and a marginal fit with correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~1|loc). The help page names four locations used as blocks, but Exam3.3 codes eight (levels c(8, 1, ..., 7)). Multivariate table: Y is row 2 and S1 row 3; count1 and count2 ('used later', no example) are ignored; A and B recode trt as a 2 x 2 factorial.

StroupGLMM Exam3.3 (Example 3.3, p. 77, 'RCBD data with fixed location effect') fits lm(Y ~ trt + loc), and Exam3.5 lm(Y ~ A + B + loc); a fixed-effects fit over blocks is rendered with random locations (mead.germination ruling).
The help page names S1 and S2 the two binomial responses over the Nbin subjects of each location and treatment; no example fits S1. Proposed: row 1's model.

RULE GAP: no example fits this table (help page: Stroup's Example 3.7, each of four batches observed at several times), and Batch has four levels. Exam2.B.6 fits the same batches as random on Table1.2, whose Y matches the rounded mean of this table's two rows per batch and time in the first rows, so Batch is kept as the grouping and the model mirrors Table1.2's row 1. Multivariate table: Fav of N is row 2 and Count row 3.

formula: cbind(Fav, N - Fav) ~ X + (1 + X || Batch)
notes: Help page: Fav the successes of N independent Bernoulli trials per batch and time; no example fits them. Proposed as row 1.
The help page calls Count a binomial response variable but names no trials for it, so it is filed as a count; no example fits it. Proposed as row 1.

StroupGLMM Exam4.1 (Stroup 2012, Example 4.1, p. 138): trt and block as factors; lmer(y ~ trt + (1|block)) by REML and by ML, beside lm(y ~ trt + block); Exam5.3 refits the same lmer for empirical standard errors. An incomplete block design of 15 blocks from Cochran and Cox (1957).

StroupGLMM Exam8.1 (Example 8.1, p. 250, nested factorial): lmer(y ~ set + trt %in% set + (1|set/block)), whose (1|set/block) expands to (1|set) + (1|set:block). The (1|set) term beside the fixed two-level set is aliased, so the row keeps the blocks-within-sets term (Cultivation ruling); set:block is block, since the ten blocks are numbered across sets. The six treatments nest in the two sets (help page), so trt %in% set codes as trt.

formula: y ~ a * b + (1 | block) + (1 | block:a) + (1 | block:b)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.2 (Example 8.2, p. 252, incomplete strip-plot, 3 x 3 factorial): block, a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a*b + (1|block) + (1|block:a) + (1|block:b)). a is assigned at random to the rows and b to the columns of each block of two rows and two columns, so row and col are the field coordinates block:a and block:b already carry.

formula: y ~ a + b + c + I(a^2) + I(b^2) + a:c + b:c + (1 | block)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.3 (Example 8.3, p. 255, response surface with incomplete blocking): three lmer fits with (1|block); fm1 adds the lack-of-fit term aa:bb:cc of factor copies of a, b and c, fm2 is the full second-order surface, and fm3, the final model whose coefficients the page plots, is y ~ a + b + c + I(a^2) + I(b^2) + a*c + b*c + (1|block).

formula: y ~ a + b %in% a + (1 | block) + (1 | block:a) + (1 | block:b)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.4 (Example 8.4, p. 259, multifactor treatment and multilevel design structures): block, a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a + b %in% a + (1|block) + (1|block:a) + (1|block:b)). a is assigned to the rows and b to the columns within blocks, so row and col are ignored as coordinates.
StroupGLMM Exam9.1 (Example 9.1, p. 273, one-way random effects only): a as a factor; lmer(y ~ 1 + (1|a)), beside lm(y ~ a) to compare the BLUPs with the fixed means; a has 12 levels (help page).

StroupGLMM Exam9.2 (Example 9.2, p. 276, two-way random effects nested model): the help page nests the levels of b within those of a, and the page's fixed version is lm(y ~ a + b %in% a), but its mixed fit lmer(y ~ (1|b/a)) nests a in b and then reads ranef(...)$a, which that fit lacks; filed as the intended (1|a/b) (an evident bug files the intended model, voorspoels).

StroupGLMM Exam9.4 (Example 9.4, p. 288, BLUP and fixed effect estimators): a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a + (1|b) + (1|a/b)), whose (1|a/b) expands to (1|a) + (1|a:b). The (1|a) term beside the fixed two-level a is aliased, so the row keeps b and a:b (Cultivation ruling).

RULE GAP: StroupGLMM Exam2.B.6 (Example 2.B.6, p. 58, 'multi batch regression data assuming different forms of linear models keeping batch effect random') fits lme(fixed = Y ~ X, random = list(Batch = pdDiag(~1), X = pdDiag(~1))), which nests a random intercept in each Batch x X cell, one row each, an alias of the residual. Filed as random intercepts and slopes per batch, the random version of Exam2.B.5's batch-specific lines (lm(Y ~ 0 + Batch + Batch/X)), uncorrelated as pdDiag makes them. Four batches. Exam1.2 plots Y by Batch. Fav of N is row 2.

formula: cbind(Fav, N - Fav) ~ X + (1 + X || Batch)
notes: Help page: Fav the successes of N Bernoulli trials per batch and time; no example fits them. Proposed as row 1.

formula: eng ~ mot + gpa + grade + rural + frpm + (1 | school)
notes: Help page: student engagement of 528 students in 40 schools, school the clustering variable, rural and frpm school-level; example data for missing data (engage.miss deletes values from it). No model on the page or in the package; the title names engagement the outcome. Proposed: every documented predictor with a school intercept. Companion of Huang, Practical Multilevel Modeling Using R (Sage), whose code sits behind the publisher's login.

MLMusingR mixPV help (examples): m1 <- mixPV(pv1math + pv2math + pv3math + pv4math + pv5math ~ escs + (1|schoolid), weights = c('w_fstuwt', 'w_fschwt'), data = pisa2012), a weighted mixed model (WeMix) fitted to each of the five plausible values and pooled; lrtPV tests it against (escs|schoolid). The row takes the first plausible value, the other four being alternate responses; the student and school weights and pwt1 (a conditional student weight) are left out of the formula. noise1 is random noise (help page). Huang (2024), Large-scale Assessments in Education 12(7).

Help page: y the outcome, w1 a level-2 and x1 a level-1 predictor, group the cluster identifier of 30 groups; 'example data for testing the need for a random intercept', which 'illustrates the need to adjust the p values for a modified LRT'. No model call on the page.
Help page: as ri_test1, with 3,000 rows in 30 groups; 'LRT results show that a random slope is not warranted', so the random-intercept model stands. No model call on the page.

formula: math ~ male + minority + mses + mhmwk + (1 | schid)
notes: MLMusingR robust_mixed help (examples): robust_mixed(lmer(math ~ male + minority + mses + mhmwk + (1|schid), data = sch29)), CR2 robust standard errors on the lmer fit. Students in 29 NELS schools; mses and mhmwk are the school means of ses and byhomewk, which stay as columns.

formula: sus ~ male + gpa + fight + pminor + (1 | school)
notes: Help page: 8465 students from 100 Virginia schools; sus the self-reported suspension, fight, male, gpa and the school's percent minority enrollment pminor. No model on the page; the title names suspension the outcome. Proposed: a logistic model with the documented predictors and a school intercept. ztc, frpmp and frpl are undocumented; the centered copies (gpa.c, pminor.c, frpm.c, frmp.c) and the school mean gpam are ignored as derived.

formula: pv1math ~ escs + othl + intmat + private + schsize + (1 | schoolid)
notes: RESPONSE INFERRED: help page: PISA students of Thailand in schools, 'example data to be used for centering', no model. thai.sm, its reduced version (excluded as derived), keeps math (the first plausible value in mathematics), escs, othl, intmat, private, schsize and schoolid, so the row takes those as the response and predictors. The reading plausible values are alternate responses and w_fstuwt the student weight.
